# Education in Sweden: Key Features and Structure
Education in Sweden is organized into several clearly defined stages: preschool (Förskola) for children aged 1–6, a free preschool class for age 6, a nine-year comprehensive compulsory school (Grundskola) for ages 7–16, followed by upper secondary school (Gymnasieskola) for ages 16–19. The compulsory school curriculum includes 16 mandatory subjects, with grading beginning at year 6. After compulsory schooling, students can attend upper secondary school, which offers 18 national programs—divided into vocational and preparatory tracks—along with introductory programs for those who do not initially qualify. Admission to upper secondary programs is competitive and based on students’ grades from lower schooling.
Higher education in Sweden consists of bachelor's (kandidatexamen, three years), master's (magister/masterexamen, one or two years), and doctoral (PhD/doktorsexamen, four years) degrees, awarded by public universities and university colleges aligned with the Bologna Process. Entrance requires proficiency in Swedish and English and is based on grades and the SweSAT aptitude test. Student aid is available through the National Board of Student Aid (CSN). Sweden also supports a system of higher vocational education and public funding for independent (friskolor/free) schools at all levels, which now enroll a significant share of students and have stimulated national debate about standards, equity, and profit.
Sweden’s education system is characterized by universal accessibility, public funding, regular national testing, and criteria-referenced grading. While the nation has historically performed well in international assessments like PISA and PIRLS, recent years have seen fluctuations in results and concerns about grade inflation and rising inequality, particularly regarding independent schools. Educational reform continues to be a subject of broad public and political interest.
